title: The Atlas specifies contract behaviour statement by statement, embedding Solidity fragments as governed procedure
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.1 breaks each admin function into individually addressed steps with the source quoted inline. `setMaxSlippage` becomes four sections: confirm the caller holds `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` (.3.1, quoting the `onlyRole` modifier), validate the bound — "the operator must ensure the provided `maxSlippage` does not exceed `1e18`, reverting with `MainnetController/max-slippage-out-of-bounds` otherwise" (.3.2) — write the mapping (.3.3), and "emit the event to the blockchain logs" (.3.4). `setMintRecipient` and `setLayerZeroRecipient` get the same treatment.

The framing is unusual and revealing: each step is written as an obligation on **the operator** ("the operator must emit the event") even where the statement is executed automatically by the contract. The Atlas is not documenting the code — it is **restating the code as procedure that a human is accountable for**, so a deviation is a governance breach rather than merely a bug.

The benefit is that the governed text and the deployed bytecode are checkable against each other at the granularity of a single require statement. A reader can verify that the contract does what the Artifact says without trusting a summary.

The cost is coupling. Every contract upgrade now implies an Artifact edit, and any drift between the two produces a document that describes a system that no longer exists. Given how many parameters in the neighbouring sections already read "will be specified in a future iteration" (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.1.1.3), that maintenance burden is not hypothetical.

It also explains the Atlas's sheer volume: at this resolution, a handful of admin setters consumes as much document space as an entire governance process.
description: Admin operations are decomposed into numbered steps — check the role, validate the bound, write the mapping, emit the event
